pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 7–8 years

- **Topic:** Where water is found on Earth

- **Standards — UK (KS1/KS2 Geography & Science — identify seas/oceans and physical features; states of matter foundation):** Children name where water is found — oceans, rivers, lakes, glaciers/ice, underground — and recognise water as liquid and as solid (ice/snow).

- **Standards — US (NGSS 2-ESS2-3):** [curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-ESS2-3].

- **Operational details:** This is a survey-and-classify concept. Build a mental map of Earth's water stores (oceans, rivers, lakes, glaciers, groundwater, and — for the readier child — the atmosphere) and tag each as liquid or solid. Two big ideas carry the weight: (1) water lives in many different places, and (2) most of Earth's water is in the oceans. Use a globe/world map so children SEE how much is blue, and photographs of each store (a glacier, a river, a lake, a well/spring) to make 'underground' and 'ice' concrete. Connect to prior state-of-matter work: glaciers and snow are the same water, just frozen solid.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete / observational). The child lists several places water is found, sorts examples into solid vs liquid (glacier/snow = solid; ocean/river = liquid), and says that most of Earth's water is in the oceans.
bestPractices: Start from a globe or world map so the dominance of ocean water is seen, not just told ('most of Earth's water is in the oceans').
Use real photographs of each store — glacier, river, lake, spring/well, snow — to make abstract locations (especially 'underground') concrete.
Explicitly tag each store as solid or liquid, linking to prior heating/cooling state-change work (ice and snow are frozen water).
Have children generate and sort their own examples ('where have YOU seen water?') into liquid/solid and into named stores.
Keep it observational and vocabulary-rich at this age; save proportions/percentages for the later salt-vs-fresh graphing topic.
keyRepresentations: A globe / world map showing oceans dominating Earth's surface.
A labelled 'water stores' picture: ocean, river, lake, glacier, groundwater, (atmosphere).
A solid-vs-liquid sorting mat for water examples.
Photo cards of each water store for classification.
commonMisconceptions: 'Most water is in rivers and lakes' — not realising oceans hold the vast majority.
'Ice/snow isn't water' — not connecting frozen forms to liquid water.
'There's no water underground' — missing groundwater as a real, large store.
'All water is drinkable/fresh' — not yet distinguishing salt ocean water from fresh water (addressed fully in the later salt-vs-fresh topic).
'Water is only where you can see it' — overlooking hidden stores (groundwater, atmospheric vapour).

learn.summary: For children aged 7–8, build a mental map of where water is found on Earth — oceans, rivers, lakes, glaciers/snow/ice, and underground (and, for readier children, the atmosphere) — and tag each store as liquid or solid. Two big ideas carry the weight: water is found in many places (seen and unseen), and most of Earth's water is in the oceans. Connect frozen forms (glaciers, snow, ice) back to prior state-of-matter work: they are the same water, just solid. Keep it observational and vocabulary-rich; save proportions/percentages for a later salt-vs-fresh graphing topic.

activities.title: Survey the cutaway Earth: tap-to-reveal water stores
feedback: If a child names rivers/lakes as holding the most water, compare the sizes directly: the oceans dwarf rivers and lakes — most of Earth's water is salty sea water.
If a child says ice or snow 'isn't really water', note that ice is water in its solid form, and connect to prior heating/cooling work (ice can melt back to liquid).
If a child overlooks groundwater, point to wells and springs as evidence that water is held underground in soil and rock.
activities.rationale: The learning objective is to survey and classify water stores and tag each as solid or liquid — a labelled mental map. A single rich, tappable scene delivers the vocabulary, one fact per store, and a solid/liquid flag without needing dynamic machinery. A globe makes ocean dominance seen rather than merely told. Interactive tap-to-reveal and lift-the-flap are concrete ways to rehearse naming and classifying; a static labelled diagram or picture cards can serve the same purpose.
sourceClaims: Most of Earth's water is in the oceans (~97% salt water); fresh water is in glaciers, groundwater, rivers and lakes.
learnerActions: Look at a globe or world map and describe how much of Earth's surface is blue (ocean).
Explore a cutaway Earth scene — globe above, ground cross-section below — with water stores to discover: ocean, river, lake, mountain glacier, snowfield, and hidden groundwater below the surface.

For each store, reveal a short fact and name the store aloud: e.g. ocean → 'oceans hold most of Earth's water, and it is salty'; glacier/snowfield → 'frozen water — the same water, just solid'; below ground → 'groundwater — hidden liquid water you can't see from the surface'.
For each store, answer a lift-the-flap 'solid or liquid?' prompt before the answer is shown.
Point to or name a store you would never have guessed held water (e.g. underground).
activities.intendedInsight: Water is found in many different places — seen and unseen, solid and liquid — and the oceans hold far more than everything else combined.

activities.title: Generate and sort your own water examples
feedback: If snow or ice is sorted as 'not water', show or recall melting an ice cube: it becomes liquid water, so it counts as water in solid form.

If a child only lists visible water, prompt for hidden stores — water held underground, and water vapour in the air, which you cannot see — to extend beyond 'water is only where you can see it'; clouds can be noted as visible signs of water in the sky, not as the invisible example.
Affirm correct sorts by restating the rule used: 'Yes — a glacier is frozen, so it goes on solid.'
activities.rationale: Having children generate and classify their own examples makes the categorisation active and vocabulary-rich, and surfaces misconceptions (ice not counting, hidden stores missed) for direct response. Real photographs make abstract locations such as 'underground' concrete.
learnerActions: Answer 'Where have YOU seen water?' and list as many places as you can (e.g. sea, puddle, tap, snow, pond, ice lolly, river).
Sort each example onto a solid-vs-liquid mat: glacier/snow/ice → solid; ocean/river/lake/puddle → liquid.
Group examples under named stores: ocean, river, lake, glacier/ice, underground, (atmosphere/clouds for readier children).
Match a store name to a photograph of that store (e.g. 'glacier' → photo of ice sheet; 'spring/well' → photo of groundwater source).
activities.intendedInsight: Every example of water belongs both to a place (store) and to a state (solid or liquid), and learners can classify their own examples, not just supplied ones.

activities.title: The jar demonstration: how much water is where
feedback: If a child picks rivers/lakes or 'drinking water' as the majority, return to the jar comparison — the big jar (oceans) dwarfs the drop or two (rivers and lakes), and even the ice cube and the spoonful of underground water.
Probe gently: 'Is the water in the sea the same kind you can drink? What's different about it?' to foreshadow the later salt-vs-fresh topic without requiring percentages now.
Probe: 'A glacier is a huge sheet of ice — is that part of Earth's water? Why?' and 'Where could water be hiding you can't see from the surface?'
activities.rationale: A concrete comparative demonstration makes the relative sizes of water stores visible, supporting the big idea that oceans hold the most. Keeping it to relative volumes (not percentages) fits the age and leaves exact proportions for later work. The jar is a rough representation, not a measurement of real global volumes. This activity also gives a two-tier check: the store (oceans) plus the state reasoning (ice counts).
sourceClaims: Most of Earth's water is in the oceans (~97% salt water); fresh water is in glaciers, groundwater, rivers and lakes.
learnerActions: Use a hands-on model where a big jar of water = the oceans, an ice cube = glaciers/ice, a spoonful = underground water, and just a drop or two = rivers and lakes.
Compare the amounts by eye and say which store holds the most.
State in your own words: 'Most of Earth's water is in the oceans; rivers and lakes are only a tiny part.'
Answer the diagnostic: 'If you gathered up ALL the water on Earth, where is most of it? And does ice count as water too?'
activities.intendedInsight: Most of Earth's water is in the oceans by a large margin; rivers and lakes are a small share; and ice is water too (solid), as is underground water.

constraints: Keep it observational and vocabulary-rich at this age; do not introduce percentages or precise proportions — save quantitative salt-vs-fresh work for the later graphing topic.

Multiple-choice/matching/sorting checks (e.g. 'Most of Earth's water is in ___') assess recognition and classification cleanly, but recognition-only items do not require a learner to generate their own examples — pair them with the open 'where have you seen water?' task for production.

A spinnable 3D globe or a drag-and-drop labelling game can motivate and add light manipulation, but the core learning (naming stores, solid vs liquid) is not inherently spatial or dynamic; treat these as optional wrappers, not the mechanism.
The salt vs fresh ocean-water distinction is only foreshadowed here, not fully taught; the full distinction belongs to the later salt-vs-fresh topic.
Hands-on melting and the jar model are approximations/representations, not measurements of real global volumes; present relative sizes, not exact figures.
When countering 'water is only where you can see it', use water held underground and water vapour in the air as the hidden examples; do not present clouds (which are visible) as the invisible store.

If the atmosphere store is included for readier children, treat it as an extension beyond the solid/liquid tagging focus, since most water in the air is invisible water vapour (a gas); clouds are made of tiny liquid droplets or ice crystals.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Both cited sources are marked verified:false in the row. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The '~97% salt water' figure appears only in the cited USGS claim and is deliberately kept out of learner-facing actions at this age (per the pedagogy guidance to defer proportions); it is retained in sourceClaims where it supports the 'oceans hold the most' principle.

The original recommendation's phrase that classification is 'rehearsed by touch' was softened: tap/lift-the-flap are concrete ways to rehearse naming and sorting, but touch is not claimed to be the only or necessary route. A static diagram or photo cards can also teach this.

The non-preferred conversation entry (persona chat 'reciting the list') was dropped as adding no distinct pedagogical purpose for a naming/classifying objective; this is a design judgement, not an evidenced efficacy claim.

Original feedback referring to 'water vapour in clouds' as a hidden store was corrected: clouds are visible condensed droplets/ice, so water vapour in the air is the accurate 'cannot-see-it' example; this fix is applied in the feedback, a dedicated constraint, and here.
Independent fresh audit found no remaining critical learner-facing errors, contradictions, or unsupported categorical modality claims; evidence/efficacy uncertainty remains appropriately hedged.

probeDeeper: Is the water in the sea the same kind you can drink? What's different about it?
A glacier is a huge sheet of ice. Is that part of Earth's water? Why?
Where could water be hiding that you can't see from the surface?
assess.correctAnswer: Most of Earth's water is in the oceans (salty sea water), by far. Rivers and lakes are only a small part. Ice — glaciers, ice caps, snow — IS water, just in solid form; water can be liquid or solid. Water is also found underground.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Most of Earth's water is fresh / in rivers and lakes'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Compare the volumes — oceans dwarf rivers and lakes; most of Earth's water is salty.
errorPatterns.distractor: Most of Earth's water is in rivers and lakes.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: names rivers, lakes or 'drinking water' as the majority

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Ice isn't really water, so glaciers don't count'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Ice is water as a solid — melt an ice cube to show it.
errorPatterns.distractor: Ice isn't really water, so glaciers don't count.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: excludes ice/glaciers from 'where water is found'

errorPatterns.nextMove: Wells and springs show water held underground in soil and rock.

responseLevels.gap: Thinks most water is in rivers/lakes or is fresh; doesn't count ice as water.
responseLevels.full: Knows most water is in the oceans (salty), that rivers and lakes are a small share, that ice is solid water, and that water is also found underground.
responseLevels.partial: Lists several places water is found but can't say the oceans hold most, or is unsure whether ice and groundwater count.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: If you could gather up ALL the water on Earth — oceans, rivers, lakes, ice and underground — where is most of it? And does ice count as water too?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who thinks most water is in rivers/lakes, or that most is fresh and drinkable, or who doesn't count ice as water, differs from one who knows the ocean holds most and that ice is solid water.

sources.claim: Most of Earth's water is in the oceans (~97% salt water); fresh water is in glaciers, groundwater, rivers and lakes.
